newsitem.title: CUBA: Canada, Cuba hold talks on human rights issues.
newsitem.headline: Canada, Cuba hold talks on human rights issues.

text.p: Canadian and Cuban officials have held two days of talks on human rights issues in Havana in a follow-up to a visit to Cuba last month by Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, a Canadian official said on Wednesday.

Canada's ambassador to Cuba, Mark Entwistle, told reporters the talks on Monday and Tuesday were a very unusual example of Cuba having a detailed discussion of human rights issues with a Western government, adding it had been a "very interesting experience".

The Canadian team, including two officials from the Foreign Ministry and a human rights expert, had met officials from the Foreign and Justice Ministries, as well as representatives of Cuban dissident groups and non-governmental organisations, he said.

The agreement to discuss human rights was included in a list of areas in which the two countries could increase cooperation that was outlined in a joint declaration issued at the end of Axworthy's visit.

Entwistle said Canada was not expecting immediate dramatic results from the talks on human rights, which are expected to continue in the coming months. Nor did it expect Cuba to take measures because Canada told it what to do, he said.

But he added it was useful to be engaged in such a dialogue. "You cannot criticise them unless you talk to them first," he said, adding "this was not a political level visit, this was a confidence-building series of discussions."

Entwistle said that while Canada believed that Cuba has had some successes in some social and economic rights, it also views Cuba as having a human rights problem, notably in the lack of freedom of expression and of association, and would like to see some progress on this.

He noted Canada protested last week to the Cuban government about government-inspired protests against dissidents. On several occasions earlier this month, small crowds gathered outside the homes of dissident journalists in Havana to shout slogans and abuse at them.

The United States, which maintains a 35-year-old economic embargo on the island, was sceptical about the usefulness of the Axworthy visit and the joint declaration. But Canada maintains it is more useful to engage in dialogue and contact with the communist-ruled island than to isolate it.
